Quantum field theory faces a notable challenge in the optimization problem, which involves finding extremal points of functionals defined on infinite-dimensional manifolds. A key step in solving this optimization problem involves deriving an equation of motion, which in the case of quantum fields, takes the form of an Euler-Arnold equation. Here, we provide a novel derivation of the Euler-Arnold equation for the time-dependent Vlasov-Schrödinger hierarchy, focusing on the Hilbert-Fock space metric. Additionally, we outline the implications of this equation for both classical and quantum field theories, highlighting its connection to the optimization problem and its role in eliminating irrelevant variables. Furthermore, we explore the underlying underlying rigorous analytical techniques, including the use of the real analysis tool, the Krylov abstract theory, to establish the well-posedness of the Euler-Arnold equation in its weak form. Moreover, we discuss the related issues of unconditional uniqueness and the conservation of key quantities, such as the energy conservation law, demonstrating the equivalence between the derived Euler-Arnold equation and the underlying hierarchy. Lastly, we provide a roadmap for extending these analytical methods to more complex, multi-component quantum field theories. 
By integrating differential geometry, analysis, and physical principles within the framework of quantum field theory, this study lays a strong foundation for resolving the optimization problem and paves the way for exploring more sophisticated theoretical models.

Furthermore, we examine how the agents will behave and learn their strategies in a scenario where the distribution of difficulty is not uniformly known and varies across different groups of tasks. We find that in a two-agent, two-action system, optimal strategy equilibrium is directly linked to the true probability of the most difficult task. If the system is not fully observable, we discover that agents will group similar tasks together and learn the group probabilities instead. We also examine a scenario where a new task arrives, and we investigate how the existing agreement between agents will be affected and how they can relearn a new equilibrium. We apply our findings to a case study involving a multi-agent system with multiple actions and multiple groups of tasks and examine how it can be used for designing such systems. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by implementing it in a realistic laboratory setting with human participants and evaluate its efficacy. Our results show that our approach is highly effective and viable even with human agents. We release our code and data on the following website: https://www.mpi-inf.mpg.de/projects/REGRET.
